title: E25 - Are Lawyers Adopting AI? With David Wong and Raghu Ramanathan
author: David Wong · Raghu Ramanathan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not substantively assess whether automation erodes apprenticeship or how expertise should be reproduced. Instead, it shifts the emphasis from replacing junior production to using AI as a supervised creative thought partner, while distinguishing brainstorming from reliable legal problem-solving and prioritising attorney experience, adoption and retention.
qs: And that creative experience and thinking through documents where it doesn't matter if it's generating a hallucination, because you're not saying, I want you to write the brief for me.
I think there is a divide between sort of general sort of common sense knowledge versus legal problem solving and knowledge.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source does not assess whether AI uptake can close the justice gap. It redirects attention to commercial-sector adoption, buyer incentives, expected—not realised—time savings, security and broader ROI, while still reinforcing the cluster’s distinction between reported use and demonstrated transformation.
qs: The other thing which I would say is more a gradual progress, last year when we surveyed the professionals and we said, how much do you expect to save in terms of time and you've done your research, Zach, they'd said 200 hours, that's roughly what they expect to save in a year.

In-house legal departments have budget problems, and for them, this is something that absolutely fits with their strategy, and they're more under pressure to adopt these tools, to show the benefits, right?

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source reports that legal AI adoption has risen and says an earlier survey informed Abramowitz’s market outlook, but it provides no figures, methodology or analysis of vendor competition, value capture, concentration or durable returns. It therefore does not establish a position on the cluster’s central proposition.
qs: I took a long look at this survey in 2024, and it was really the basis of a lot of our theses and our view of the market of where AI was going in legal.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the need for business-model and process redesign and materially extends the cluster with survey-based evidence that in-house teams’ budget incentives support faster adoption, plus customer observations that smaller firms are pursuing more ambitious operational change. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution by distinguishing perceived benefits and customer reports from measured outcomes, though it does not address pricing, verification or apprenticeship in depth.
qs: In-house legal departments have budget problems, and for them, this is something that absolutely fits with their strategy, and they're more under pressure to adopt these tools, to show the benefits, right?

And we're seeing adoption of our solutions, but also other AI solutions in niche spaces like personal injury and in smaller firms where they're trying to completely upend the business model or the process to be much more tech oriented.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on effective organisational adoption rather than access alone, emphasising tool fit, user experience and practical helpfulness. It materially extends the cluster by identifying attorney and client retention—and future recruitment—as additional, though largely predictive, dimensions of institutional absorption and ROI.
qs: So I think that, you know, when I think about the ROI, I think it may ultimately come down both to preventing client churn and attorney churn, which is to say that a big firm today or maybe, you know, year and two years from now that has an antiquated approach to AI may see it really difficult to recruit the best staff.
Like adoption is driven by which solutions are the most delightful, but also the ones that are just frankly the most helpful, even if it's not going to be in the same sort of measurable way.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source aligns with selective, judgment-led adoption and materially extends the cluster’s implementation account. It identifies leadership example as an organisational adoption mechanism and adds user-base evidence that AI usage is not correlated with age, tentatively explaining this through a balance between faster initial learning and experienced lawyers’ stronger use-case judgment. It does not independently address verification costs or productivity gains.
qs: That has a way of impacting the rest of the organization when it's at the very top levels.

But also, I would say the reason why the correlation is not there is, the more experienced lawyers probably know how to use it from a use-case perspective in the right way, which the newer lawyers need to learn.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s near-term impact is primarily on how legal work is produced and organised, citing time savings, lower costs, implementation-dependent business-model change and faster in-house adoption. It materially extends the cluster by framing lawyer-in-the-loop AI as an on-demand legal thought partner and by adding user experience, client retention and lawyer recruitment as strategic sources of value beyond production efficiency.
qs: But we certainly are hearing that as well, that it's both about doing the work with higher quality as well as doing the same work for lower time and cost.

But one thing which I would say is that we look at how people are using a lot of these tools and you kind of say like, hey, how do I have like a thought partner or something that can help me with problem solving, et cetera?

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s cautious account of immature, bounded agentic deployment. It provides a concrete example of a legal-specific agent integrated with Copilot and anticipates operational mishaps, but offers no measured evidence or direct analysis of verification bottlenecks.
qs: Which is to say, there's some clunkiness to work out.

We actually developed by today's terms, what you call a legal agent, which sits with Copilot, and Copilot can draw upon for legal specific questions, which was highlighted in Microsoft's big conference.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that practical legal-AI value depends on domain-specific tools and complementary human use rather than autonomous, general-purpose generation. Its emphasis on immature agents and AI-assisted brainstorming reinforces retained lawyer involvement, although its claims rely on examples and anecdote rather than comparative validation.
qs: I think what we're seeing is that general purpose tools can solve a broad set of use cases, but once you want to create something which is tuned for your domain or for your work, you can provably get better performance if you have a company or a startup, or someone that's building something specific.
And that creative experience and thinking through documents where it doesn't matter if it's generating a hallucination, because you're not saying, I want you to write the brief for me.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s conditional framing by distinguishing perceived reliability and verification needs across legal-specific and general-purpose AI. Its claims are reported user confidence, supplemented by an analogy about review expectations, rather than measured evidence that CoCounsel is accurate enough to eliminate verification.
qs: They were saying, look, it's interesting for me to see how a Claude thinks and an OpenAI deep research thinks, but I know that when I look at the answers from co-counsel, that this is a lot more reliable.

I don't have to double-check it, whereas anything I get from Anthropic or OpenAI deep research, it opens my thinking, but I need to go and validate everything because I'm not 100% sure if it is all accurate.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified account of in-house legal departments as increasingly important AI buyers: it reports higher day-to-day use among in-house lawyers and attributes uptake to budget pressure, enterprise resources and leadership. It also supports coexistence between general-purpose and specialised legal tools. It does not directly show work being insourced or outside-counsel spending declining, so its support is strongest on adoption and buyer incentives rather than substitution.
qs: But again, if you step back, an industry where has gone from a low single-digit percentage usage of AI among legal professionals to now 35 or 45 percent, depending on the law firms in-house legal council, that's just simply incredible.

In-house legal departments have budget problems, and for them, this is something that absolutely fits with their strategy, and they're more under pressure to adopt these tools, to show the benefits, right?

st.t: Legal consolidation: Acquisitions create integration work first
st.an: Thomson Reuters supports the cluster’s integrated-capabilities framing by presenting build, buy and partner as complementary choices and describing CoCounsel as a way to connect its existing tools, skills, data and content. It also supports acquisitions and specialist partnerships as routes to innovation, while offering strategic rationale rather than evidence of completed integration, comparative performance or post-acquisition organisational work.
qs: And we've said before, we have a three-pronged strategy here, which is we're going to build, we're going to buy, we're going to partner, and we'll do it when each of those tactics makes the most sense for the time for Reuters.

It would be better for our customers if we had a single legal AI system, which could then access and take advantage of the different tools, the different skills, the different data and content that we had at TR.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, human-centred deployment: it presents AI as an assistant delivering substantial task-level time savings, while stressing task suitability, specialist legal tools, user experience and organisational strategy. Its claims are more optimistic and vendor-linked than the synthesis, and it gives limited attention to verification, but it does not claim general legal competence or wholesale lawyer replacement.
qs: It's like we've given everyone this amazing assistant that in some ways is not as good as a human, but in some ways is far better than a human.

So one of the things that we do, again, because we have a luxury of having hundreds of thousands of lawyers using our AI solutions and we have the data in our products and our systems, and we see how they use it, and we are seeing on an average for legal tasks anywhere from 40 to 60 percent savings in time for typical tasks, like creating a legal timeline, right?

kp.k: Reported AI adoption rises, with in-house teams ahead
kp.d: Raghu Ramanathan describes the survey as measuring professionals' day-to-day generative AI use, not surveying companies or decision-makers about vendors. He reports growth from low single-digit usage at the beginning of the previous year to roughly 35 percent in law firms and 45 percent in-house, although he initially describes the figures as firm adoption and qualifies the precise in-house gap. No sample size or detailed methodology is supplied in the conversation.
qs: the survey that we did is a survey of professionals, not of companies, not of decision makers
do you use as a professional AI in your day-to-day work, Gen. AI tools in particular, right?
now 35 or 45 percent, depending on the law firms in-house legal council

kp.k: Cost pressure and corporate infrastructure explain in-house adoption
kp.d: Ramanathan attributes faster in-house uptake to budget pressure and larger corporate AI programmes, contrasting this with law firms. David Wong adds that corporate CEOs push adoption more aggressively than managing partners and that legal departments are often asked to use enterprise-wide general tools while also considering legal-specific products. These are the speakers' explanations, rather than separately demonstrated survey findings.
qs: In-house legal departments are under enormous cost pressure. Law firms are not under cost pressure.
When you go to corporates, they have much larger budgets, they have bigger AI programs, they have much more investment.
they're being asked to use some general tool that's being provided for the corporation, and then they're also taking a look at the vertical or the function-specific tools.

kp.k: Expected annual time savings increase to 240 hours
kp.d: Ramanathan reports respondents' expected annual savings rising from 200 to 240 hours, a 20 percent increase, interpreting this as optimism rather than reporting realised savings. He extrapolates 240 hours into about $19,000 per professional annually and approximately $20 billion across about a million US lawyers. These monetary figures are his extrapolations, not measured sector-wide savings.
qs: they'd said 200 hours, that's roughly what they expect to save in a year. Now they're saying it's 240 hours. It's jumped up, it's a 20 percent jump.
that equates to about $19,000 of savings in a year.
I believe we have about a million lawyers in the US, that's about $20 billion in terms of efforts saved by JNAI across the legal sector.

kp.k: Clear AI strategy correlates with perceived benefits
kp.d: Ramanathan reports that professionals whose organisations have a clear AI strategy are 3.9 times more likely to perceive benefits. He explicitly frames this as respondents' views. Less systematic follow-up associated strategy with early implementation and engaged leadership; Wong adds understanding business impact and ROI. The discussion does not establish causation or a standardised definition of strategy.
qs: this is not our view, it's the view of the professionals
they feel that they're 3.9 times more likely to feel that are benefits coming from it
we didn't do it as systematically as rest of the survey
Most of the time, it's I understand what the business impact is going to be for my firm or for my company.

kp.k: Leadership engagement matters more than age-based adoption assumptions
kp.d: Drawing on Thomson Reuters product-use data separately from the survey, Ramanathan says repeated analysis found no correlation between age and AI usage. He agrees millennials initially learn faster but suggests experienced lawyers better understand appropriate use cases. He offers no managing-partner adoption percentage, instead reporting individual variation and observing stronger organisational movement when managing partners model use.
qs: this was not part of the survey
there is no correlation between age and usage of AI solutions among our user base.
millennials tend to pick it up quicker.
the more experienced lawyers probably know how to use it from a use-case perspective in the right way
Where we see the managing partners make themselves a personal example, this moves the law firm significantly.

kp.k: Vendor data and customer examples emphasise task-time reductions
kp.d: Ramanathan reports Thomson Reuters observations of average time savings of 40–60 percent for typical legal tasks and a company benchmark showing legal timelines produced 78 percent faster. He cites an unnamed approximately 1,000-person firm publicly reporting 6,000 lawyer hours saved in one quarter, or six hours per lawyer, and another approaching half a day saved weekly. These vendor claims and customer examples are distinct from survey expectations; underlying benchmark methods are not provided.
qs: we are seeing on an average for legal tasks anywhere from 40 to 60 percent savings in time for typical tasks
Our benchmark shows that creating a legal timeline, you can do 78 percent faster
they saved 6,000 hours of lawyer time
they saved six hours per lawyer that quarter
they're pretty close to saving about half a day in a work week for a lawyer

kp.k: Reduced staffing needs remain a conditional customer prediction
kp.d: Ramanathan recounts an unnamed managing partner predicting that the same work could be performed with 20 percent fewer lawyers within a few years. The statement is explicitly conditional on holding the firm's activities constant, and the partner's pitch anticipated becoming a different business rather than simply maintaining today's work. It is not evidence of realised job cuts.
qs: I'm convinced that what we do today, we can do it with 20 percent less lawyers, if that's all we do in a few years time
Part of the pitch is to say we won't be doing just what we're doing today

kp.k: Quality benefits exceed what current ROI measures capture
kp.d: Wong identifies time savings as the most measurable return but says survey respondents and customers also report creativity, fewer errors, improved work quality and greater chances of winning adversarial matters. He acknowledges these benefits are harder to quantify. Host Zach Abramowitz questions whether efficiencies yet reduce client bills or improve firm profits; the guests primarily answer with time-saving evidence rather than quantified financial outcomes.
qs: It's the most measurable thing that you can get.
They talk about more creativity, fewer errors, being able to be more likely to win in an adversarial situation.
They're harder to quantify though.
But it's not like it's decreasing the bill to the clients.

kp.k: Smaller firms experiment with deeper business-model changes
kp.d: Wong distinguishes modest automation of routine work from redesigning firm operations, reporting more ambitious experimentation among smaller firms, including personal injury practices, than at the top end. Ramanathan attributes faster decisions to decision-makers also being users. His example of a litigation customer handling a million documents delivered Friday before a Monday hearing and winning is a customer attribution carried by the vendor, not independently demonstrated evidence that AI caused the result.
qs: That smaller firms are much more willing to sort of turn around the model.
in niche spaces like personal injury and in smaller firms where they're trying to completely upend the business model or the process to be much more tech oriented.
the people you talk to on the other side are effectively the decision makers and the users
the defendant party came and dumped a million documents digitally on Friday evening.
win the case on Monday, and he really attributes it to JNAI.

kp.k: Host frames AI as creative support and retention infrastructure
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that AI differs from management-oriented enterprise software by directly helping individual professionals. He emphasises always-available brainstorming and critique rather than only routine-work automation, and predicts outdated AI provision could impair recruitment and contribute to client or lawyer churn over the next year or two. These are the host's qualitative arguments and predictions, not survey findings.
qs: AI really is going back to the person.
there isn't always someone that you can immediately brainstorm with on demand.
I think it may ultimately come down both to preventing client churn and attorney churn
a big firm today or maybe, you know, year and two years from now that has an antiquated approach to AI may see it really difficult to recruit the best staff.

kp.k: General and specialist AI coexist while increasingly competing
kp.d: Wong describes foundation-model providers as competitors for legal use cases while observing that lawyers use general tools for general information and specialist tools for legal reasoning. Ramanathan links movement toward function-specific products to security and privacy caution. Their argument for specialist products rests on domain content, tailored functionality and perceived reliability, rather than an expectation that lawyers will use only one category.
qs: it is now increasingly competitive, not just between the legal providers, but also with the horizontal providers.
They do not want to dabble with tools where they enter data, where they do not understand the security, the privacy behind this.
they go to a legal specific tool when they want to have someone to problem solve
They're going to have the general purpose models. They're going to have the legal models like co-counsel. They're going to have both.

kp.k: Agent integration creates opportunities and competitive tensions
kp.d: Wong says customers want assistants and agents to interact, but integration decisions remain early and complicated by foundation-model companies competing for the same buyers. Ramanathan reports an existing legal-agent collaboration with Microsoft Copilot. He distinguishes potential CoCounsel platform integration from providing AI companies raw access to Westlaw or Practical Law content, which he says is not Thomson Reuters' strategy.
qs: people want agents and assistants to be able to interact with each other. But I think it's still pretty early.
they're trying to earn the business of the same customers and trying to solve many of the same problems.
We actually developed by today's terms, what you call a legal agent, which sits with Copilot
it will not be our strategy to provide a raw access to our VEST law content
we will think about how co-counsel as a technology, as a platform, as an agent can plug in with other technology providers.

kp.k: AI threatens incumbents' core retrieval and document-production businesses
kp.d: Responding to the host's question about disruption risk, Wong explicitly describes AI as both threat and opportunity. He says Thomson Reuters products could become obsolete without investment because generative AI addresses their central functions: information retrieval and work-product production. He presents aggressive product investment as a response to that exposure.
qs: at Thomson Reuters, if we don't invest in AI, then our solutions will become obsolete.
our two basic kind of jobs, which is information retrieval and document production or kind of work product production.
we absolutely see it as both a risk and an opportunity.

kp.k: Build-buy-partner strategy targets integrated specialist capabilities
kp.d: Wong describes acquisitions and partnerships as ways to accelerate development and amplify existing technology, content and products within one legal AI system. Ramanathan states a strategic belief that domain-specific AI will win, extending this to narrower specialisms within law and citing a capital-markets-focused partner. Both stress integrating specialised capabilities into a simpler user experience; superiority of domain-specific AI is their strategic thesis rather than an independently established market outcome.
qs: we're going to build, we're going to buy, we're going to partner
We really look at trying to acquire technology and products where we get an outsize impact to everything else that we're doing at TR.
a single legal AI system, which could then access and take advantage of the different tools, the different skills, the different data and content that we had at TR.
our firm belief is that domain-specific AI will win.
to provide that micro-expertice to give it under the umbrella of a delightful, simplified user experience

kp.k: Reliability and verification claims rely on customer perceptions
kp.d: Ramanathan recounts a lawyer using both general models and CoCounsel: general-model answers broaden thinking but require validation, whereas the customer regards CoCounsel as more reliable and says double-checking is unnecessary. This is an anecdotal customer claim relayed by a vendor executive, not a measured hallucination comparison or demonstrated basis for dispensing with human verification. Abramowitz analogises the distinction to reviewing paralegal versus junior-lawyer work.
qs: I know that when I look at the answers from co-counsel, that this is a lot more reliable. There's far less hallucination. I don't have to double-check it
anything I get from Anthropic or OpenAI deep research, it opens my thinking, but I need to go and validate everything because I'm not 100% sure if it is all accurate.
it's the difference between reviewing the work of a paralegal.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Raghu Ramanathan reports a sharp rise in generative-AI adoption, with in-house lawyers ahead of law-firm lawyers.
pts.d: At 05:48–09:49, Ramanathan compares low-single-digit adoption at the beginning of 2024 with approximately 35% among law-firm professionals and 45% among in-house professionals in the current survey. Although he sometimes describes these as percentages of firms, he expressly identifies the survey population as professionals and the question as personal day-to-day use. He attributes faster in-house adoption to budget pressure. At 11:19–14:13, he and David Wong also identify larger corporate AI programmes and stronger executive pressure as contributing factors. These explanations are interview interpretations rather than reported causal survey findings.

pts.k: Ramanathan reports higher expected annual time savings and extrapolates a substantial aggregate economic value.
pts.d: At 07:48–09:49, Ramanathan says professionals' expected annual savings rose from roughly 200 hours in the previous survey to 240 hours in the current survey, a 20% increase. He interprets this as increased confidence and optimism, not as a measured annual productivity outcome. Using unspecified average rates, he translates the expectation into approximately $19,000 per professional annually and, assuming about one million US lawyers, approximately $20 billion in sector-wide effort saved. This is a conditional extrapolation, not demonstrated cash savings, client fee reductions or additional profit.

pts.k: Ramanathan says professionals reporting a clear organisational AI strategy are 3.9 times more likely to perceive benefits.
pts.d: At 19:11–21:28, Ramanathan attributes this association to the Future of Professionals survey and explicitly describes it as professionals' views. Follow-up exploration of what strategy means was less systematic than the survey. He identifies willingness to move early and hands-on leadership as important components, arguing that fast-to-deploy cloud AI changes the rationale for waiting on technology adoption. At 23:50–24:41, Wong adds that a strategy increasingly includes understanding anticipated business impact rather than merely having an experimentation plan. The reported multiplier concerns perceived benefits and does not establish a causal return on investment.

pts.k: Ramanathan says age does not correlate with AI usage in Thomson Reuters' user base, while visible managing-partner involvement promotes adoption.
pts.d: At 22:10–23:50, Ramanathan distinguishes internal product-usage analysis from the survey. He says repeated examination did not support the initial hypothesis that younger lawyers would use AI more. He accepts that millennials may learn the tools faster initially and suggests experienced lawyers' stronger use-case knowledge offsets that advantage. This balancing explanation is his interpretation. He supplies no percentage of managing partners using AI and identifies no general adoption pattern for that role. His claim that leadership example moves a firm rests on observed customer experience.

pts.k: Ramanathan presents task-level time reductions and customer-reported hours saved as the most immediate evidence of AI's value.
pts.d: At 25:19–27:55, Ramanathan cites Thomson Reuters' product data and benchmarks for average time savings of 40–60% on legal tasks and 78% faster legal-timeline creation. He also reports an unnamed roughly 1,000-person firm's public statement that it saved 6,000 lawyer hours in one quarter, which he describes as six hours per lawyer, and another firm's claim that it is approaching half a working day saved per lawyer each week. These are different measures and populations, not a single estimate of profession-wide productivity. Benchmark methods, task mix and checking requirements are not supplied. Ramanathan also recounts a managing partner's conditional prediction of needing 20% fewer lawyers within a few years if work remained unchanged; that prediction is presented as the customer's statement, not an independently established workforce forecast.

pts.k: Wong says AI's benefits extend beyond speed to perceived quality, creativity, fewer errors and stronger adversarial performance.
pts.d: At 27:57–29:54, Wong attributes these benefits to survey responses and customer conversations. He endorses them as real but explicitly says they are harder to quantify than time savings. The affected parties are lawyers, firms and corporate legal teams seeking better work product as well as lower time and cost. At 29:54–31:25, Ramanathan offers supporting customer testimony: an unnamed litigation lawyer reportedly used AI to handle a million-document Friday-evening production before a Monday court appearance and attributed winning the case to AI. This is an illustrative customer account, not a measured causal estimate of litigation outcomes.

pts.k: Wong and Ramanathan see smaller firms as especially nimble adopters and a source of more radical AI-enabled business-model change.
pts.d: At 27:57–31:25, Wong distinguishes modest automation of routine work from efforts to transform a firm's operations. Drawing primarily on customer conversations rather than the survey, he says the latter is more visible in small firms and niches such as personal injury than at the top end of the market. Ramanathan says small and medium firms can move faster because decision makers are also users, reducing deliberation. The litigation example illustrates their claim that AI can help smaller practices handle work that would otherwise overwhelm them when opposing large firms. They provide no quantified comparison of adoption speed or business-model outcomes by firm size.

pts.k: Wong says useful, enjoyable assistance drives adoption even where benefits are not readily measurable.
pts.d: At 35:07–36:55, Wong endorses the observed importance of helpfulness and user experience, including AI as a thought partner. He says customers differentiate between general-information tasks handled with general-purpose tools and legal reasoning or debate handled with legal-specific tools. This describes current customer behaviour and a developing division of labour among assistants. The host's separate prediction about client and attorney churn is not established as an interviewee finding.

pts.k: Wong and Ramanathan predict lasting value for domain-specific and narrowly specialised legal AI, while allowing coexistence with general-purpose tools.
pts.d: At 11:19–14:13 and 41:45–46:31, Ramanathan argues that function-specific AI is gaining ground because it adds relevant content and functional specialisation over foundation models, alongside users' security and privacy concerns. He predicts domain-specific AI will win and extends the thesis to narrower legal niches, citing Noetika's financing and capital-markets focus. Wong argues that purpose-built products can achieve better performance than general tools on specialised work, but supplies no comparative benchmark results here. Ramanathan explicitly says lawyers will use both general-purpose and legal-specific tools. His closing reliability example is one customer's account of greater trust in CoCounsel and less need to check its answers; it is not a measured hallucination-rate result or a demonstrated removal of human verification.

pts.k: Wong says agent interoperability creates new integration possibilities, but competition with foundation-model providers complicates the emerging ecosystem.
pts.d: At 13:08–18:11, Wong says general-purpose providers increasingly compete for legal use cases and customers. Agents open possibilities for assistants to interact, but he describes decisions about unified versus purpose-built systems as unresolved and early-stage. Ramanathan cites an existing Microsoft collaboration involving a legal agent accessible through Copilot. He states that Thomson Reuters is open to integrating CoCounsel as technology or an agent, but not to offering raw Westlaw or Practical Law content to AI providers. These claims affect legal buyers' tool choices and relationships among legal-technology vendors and general-purpose AI providers, not the delivery of legal work by ALSPs.

pts.k: Wong says generative AI threatens incumbent legal-information products with obsolescence unless they invest, while also enabling integrated new products.
pts.d: At 38:17–41:45, Wong argues that information retrieval and document or work-product production—the core functions of Thomson Reuters' products—are precisely activities generative AI handles well. He frames obsolescence as conditional on failure to invest, without specifying a deadline. He describes building, buying and partnering as the response. He explains the Casetext/CoCounsel acquisition as a means to provide one legal AI system accessing Thomson Reuters' different tools, skills, data and content, and says acquisitions are selected for their wider product and customer benefits. The evidence is executive strategy and product-market reasoning rather than measured market-share displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The interview combines professional self-reports, proprietary usage data and benchmarks, customer anecdotes, and executive market predictions.
pts.d: The survey supports reported use, expected savings and perceived strategy-related benefits. Internal Thomson Reuters analysis supports the stated age-usage finding and task-time claims. Customer accounts illustrate realised hours saved, litigation assistance and differing implementation strategies. Predictions about domain-specific AI, incumbent obsolescence and market integration rest on the interviewees' commercial experience and reasoning.
